The QMSR Timeline, 2022 to 2026

There are 7 points on this timeline, and I want to walk them in order because the sequence explains why enforcement arrived as quickly as it did.

The proposed rule published on February 23, 2022 at 87 FR 10119, and comments closed on May 24, 2022. The final rule published on February 2, 2024 at 89 FR 7496, incorporating ISO 13485:2016 by reference, and FDA's frequently asked questions page describes that rule as issued January 31, 2024, which is the public-inspection date rather than the publication date. On October 15, 2024 a correction restored the "batch or lot" definition in 820.3(a), which had been left out of the codified text. Then on December 4, 2025 the technical amendments published at 90 FR 55978, and those re-pointed 179 sections across 18 CFR parts from the old Quality System Regulation, or QSR, citations to 820.35 and 820.10(c), which was purely conforming work and added no new obligations.

FDA then spent the winter explaining the rule. The agency ran a Key Takeaways webinar on December 16, 2025 and town halls on January 14 and April 1, 2026, covering risk, design, and inspections. On February 2, 2026 the rule took effect, QSIT was withdrawn, and Compliance Program 7382.850 replaced Compliance Program 7382.845 and Compliance Program 7383.001. The compliance program's own cover page says issued February 2, 2026, while law firms reported it posted on January 30, and either way it applied from day one.

Then come the Warning Letters. The first Warning Letters arising from QMSR inspections went to Linemaster Switch on May 27, 2026, Koven Technologies on July 21, and Nipro Renal Solutions USA on July 24. Finally, at the town hall on April 1, 2026, FDA put it plainly, stating that "The transition period has ended ... companies need to be compliant with the QMSR now."

The New Part 820 on One Slide

In order to work out what your own system now has to look like, you have to start from what the regulation actually says today. The whole of Part 820 is now 6 operative sections, and everything else is ISO 13485:2016, clauses 4 through 8, read together with the standard's Introduction, which means Clauses 0.1, 0.2, and 0.4 are incorporated as well, while the ISO notes explain the requirements without adding to them.

820.1 sets the scope, which covers finished devices for human use, including human cells, tissues, and cellular and tissue-based products, or HCT/Ps, that are regulated as devices, and components remain excluded. The check in your own system is whether the scope statement in your manual cites both 21 CFR 820 and ISO 13485:2016, and names the roles you actually perform.

820.3 handles definitions. The ISO 13485 and ISO 9000 Clause 3 definitions now apply, paragraph (a) keeps 6 FDA-only terms, and paragraph (b) provides that the definitions in section 201 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act prevail, along with 5 superseding terms, and no procedure of yours should still be relying on a definition which was dropped.

820.7 is the incorporation by reference, bringing in ISO 13485:2016(E), third edition, together with Clause 3 of ISO 9000:2015, both of which are readable at no cost through the ANSI portal, so the question is whether a controlled copy reaches the people who need it.

820.10 carries the requirements. Paragraph (a) requires you to document a quality management system, or QMS, complying with ISO 13485, and paragraph (b) is the set of hooks into the rest of Title 21, specifically Parts 830, 821, 803, and 806. Paragraph (c) requires Clause 7.3 for Class II, Class III, and listed Class I devices, paragraph (d) applies Clause 7.5.9.2 to life-supporting devices, and paragraph (e) provides that noncompliance renders a device "adulterated". What that translates into is a procedure index mapped to the ISO clauses and to the 820.10(b) hooks, along with a documented 7.3 decision.

820.35 adds FDA-specific content on top of Clause 4.2.5, covering complaint and servicing record content, unique device identification, or UDI, per device or batch, and confidentiality marking, while 820.45 adds to Clause 7.5.1, requiring documented procedures, a 5-point examination before release, a documented release, and mix-up prevention.

The remaining sections are reserved, and those are the following: 820.5, 820.20 through 820.30, 820.40, and Subparts C through O. There is no action in the placeholders themselves. However, there is very much an action in your own documents, which is the old citations to those sections still sitting inside your procedures.

Which Definition Wins

In order to read the new Part 820 correctly, you have to work through 4 layers of definitions in a fixed order, and that order decides which word governs where the regulation and the standard differ. The first layer is the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act itself, and the section 201 definitions prevail over the correlating ISO terms, which means that "device" governs over "medical device" and "labeling" governs over "labelling" in every instance. The second layer is the 5 superseding terms that FDA placed into 820.3(b), which include: implantable medical device, defined by pointing back to "implant" at 21 CFR 860.3, manufacturer, organization, rework, which FDA defines as work done before release for distribution and in accordance with the medical device file, and safety and performance.

The third layer is the 6 FDA-only terms at 820.3(a), which include: batch or lot, component, Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, finished device, HCT/P regulated as a device, and remanufacturer. The fourth layer is everything else, and everything else comes from ISO 13485 Clause 3 and ISO 9000 Clause 3, which covers customer, top management, nonconformity, verification, validation, product, correction, corrective action, preventive action, risk, and the rest of the working vocabulary.

I want to highlight what FDA dropped between the proposed rule and the final rule. You will note below that the 820.15 deletion we just discussed appears on this slide as well, with its content moved into 820.3(b). The proposed definitions for customer, design validation, nonconformity, process agent, process validation, top management, and verification were all removed, so the ISO definitions apply instead. The proposed requirement to sign and date every approved record was also removed, although where ISO 13485 says "approved" that still means signed and dated, and electronic signatures are acceptable.

There are 2 traps buried in this hierarchy. "Organization" in the standard means "manufacturer" as FDA defines it, which pulls in contract sterilizers, relabelers, specification developers, and initial distributors of foreign entities. And "safety and performance" is read as "safety and effectiveness" only in Clause 0.1 of the Introduction, which FDA narrowed in the final rule after commenters pointed out that the 2 phrases are not interchangeable. In practice, do not rewrite your design inputs, and do make sure that your quality management system, or QMS, demonstrably assures safety and effectiveness. All of this sits in 21 CFR 820.3 as in force, and at 89 FR 7496, Comments 22 to 29 and 51.

What Disappeared, and Where It Went

A good deal of the old Part 820 did not so much move to a new clause as stop existing as a defined term, and the fastest way through this table is to take it in 3 groups.

The record types went first. There is no longer a device master record, a design history file, a device history record, or a quality system record as a defined term anywhere in Part 820. FDA's reasoning in Comment 31 is that the elements of each of those records are already required by ISO 13485 Clause 4.2 and by Clause 7. The content of the old device master record at 820.181 now lives in the medical device file at Clause 4.2.3, which has to hold the specifications, procedures, and requirements that are current on the floor. The design history file, or DHF, from old 820.30(j) becomes the design and development file at Clause 7.3.10. The device history record content from old 820.184 sits in the medical device or batch records under Clause 7.5.1, read together with 7.5.8 and 7.5.9, and the unique device identifier is now recorded under 820.35(c). The old quality system record at 820.186 is replaced by QMS documentation under Clause 4.2, which covers the quality manual at 4.2.2, documents at 4.2.4, and records at 4.2.5.

The exemption went next, and this is the row I would stop on. Old 820.180(c) kept management review reports, quality audit reports, and supplier audit reports out of routine FDA review. That exemption is gone, which FDA addressed in Comment 55, and FDA's FAQ number 8 says plainly that the agency has authority to inspect those records. Expect them in baseline surveillance inspections and in premarket approval, or PMA, preapproval inspections.

Then a set of smaller changes. "Management with executive responsibility" becomes "top management" under the ISO 9000 definition, while the expectation of executive-led quality culture is unchanged. The explicit independent design reviewer of old 820.30(e) is not carried over, and Clause 7.3.5 governs instead, which calls for representatives of the functions concerned plus other specialist personnel. Statistical techniques at old 820.250 became analysis of data at Clause 8.4. Corrective and preventive action, which sat in one section at old 820.100, is 2 clauses again, corrective action at 8.5.2 and preventive action at 8.5.3, both sitting under Improvement at 8.5. And QSIT itself, along with Compliance Program 7382.845 and Compliance Program 7383.001, is replaced by Compliance Program 7382.850, which brings 6 QMS Areas, 4 Other Applicable FDA Requirements, and 2 inspection models.

FDA stated its position on legacy documents at the town hall on April 1, 2026. There is no need to revise or recreate records created before 2026, and no need to scrub terms such as design history file and device master record out of documents you already have. What Did Not Change

The left column here is the reassurance, and the right column is the warning.

Starting with certification. FDA does not require ISO 13485 certification, will not accept a certificate in lieu of an inspection or an establishment inspection report, and will not issue certificates of conformity itself, which the agency addressed in Comments 79 to 81 and repeated in FAQ number 13. At the town hall on April 1, 2026 FDA added that a notified body audit does not replace your own internal audit under Clause 8.2.4, which catches firms who assumed the 2 could be merged.

The Medical Device Single Audit Program, or MDSAP, continues in the form you already know. FDA continues to use MDSAP audit reports in place of routine surveillance inspections, and sites that are actively enrolled are not scheduled for surveillance inspections, while remaining subject to for-cause inspections, compliance follow-up inspections, specific product risk inspections, and PMA inspections, which is set out in Compliance Program 7382.850 at Part I.9 and Figure 3.

Parts 803, 806, 821, and 830 are unchanged, and they are now hooked into the QMS through 820.10(b), while Part 11 is untouched. The scope of "manufacturer" is unchanged, and it should be noted that this scope has always reached beyond the finished device maker to contract sterilizers, relabelers, specification developers, and initial distributors of foreign entities. The Class I current good manufacturing practice, or CGMP, exemptions are retained, and exempt firms still keep complaint files and 820.35 records. Design and development applicability is preserved for Class II, Class III, and the listed Class I devices.

The right column is shorter and it matters more. The 2 year transition is over, and there is no phase-in, no grace period, and no enforcement discretion announced. Every inspection since February 2, 2026 is conducted to the QMSR, including compliance follow-ups after Warning Letters or consent decrees. The compliance-action threshold has not changed, and the Situation 1 examples, which are FDA's own examples of the conduct that warrants compliance action, were simply updated for the QMSR. Records created before February 2, 2026 are "fair game" if the inspection leads there. And old QSR citations still sitting in your procedures, your audit checklists, and your 483 responses are read by investigators as an incomplete transition.

820.10 and the Hooks Into the Rest of Title 21

820.10(b) is the bridge between the standard's phrase "applicable regulatory requirements" and specific FDA regulations, and FDA stated in Comment 44 that the list is not comprehensive, so manufacturers remain responsible for identifying every applicable requirement, including Part 807 registration and listing, which is not named here.

The hooks in 820.10(b) are the following: Unique Device Identification, or UDI, assignment, product tracking, reporting to FDA, and advisory notices. Paragraph (b)(1) attaches to Clause 7.5.8 and requires a documented system that assigns a UDI in accordance with Part 830, and the investigator will test that against your UDI procedure, your Global Unique Device Identification Database, or GUDID, records, the labels themselves, and the UDI recorded for each device or batch under 820.35(c). Records With FDA-Specific Content

820.35 sits on top of Clause 4.2.5, the clause that governs records generally, and it adds back the content FDA has always required for complaints, for servicing, and for UDI. The elements required for a complaint record under 820.35(a) include: the name of the device, the date the complaint was received, any UDI or Universal Product Code, or UPC, and any other device identification, the name, address, and telephone number of the complainant, the nature and details of the complaint, any correction or corrective action taken, and any reply to the complainant. That is 7 elements, and the rule then requires the record of the review, the evaluation, and the investigation, or a documented justification where a similar complaint has already been investigated and a new investigation is not performed. It is important to know that this content applies to complaints that must be reported under Part 803, to complaints you decide to investigate, and to complaints you investigated anyway.

Servicing records under 820.35(b) carry 6 elements, which include: the name of the device serviced, any UDI or UPC and other device identification, the date of service, the individual or individuals who serviced the device, the service performed, and any test and inspection data. FDA clarified in Comment 54 that the test and inspection data are required only where your process actually generates them, and Clause 7.5.4 then closes the loop, because servicing records must be analyzed to decide whether what you are holding is in fact a complaint.

820.35(c) requires the UDI to be recorded for each medical device or batch, in addition to Clauses 7.5.1, 7.5.8, and 7.5.9, and it is not required for devices under development. 820.35(d) allows records you consider confidential to be marked as such, which aids FDA's disclosure decisions under Part 20. Mark them in advance of the inspection, because a confidentiality marking isn't a shield against review.

One requirement did not survive from the proposal to the final rule, which was the signature and date on every record, and FDA's position is that "approved" means signed and dated, with electronic methods acceptable. Labeling and Packaging Controls

FDA kept 820.45 because Clause 7.5.1(e) of ISO 13485 says only that defined labeling and packaging operations must be implemented, and because labeling and packaging errors drive recalls every year, which is set out in Comments 60 and 64.

The items 820.45(a) requires to be examined for accuracy before release or storage include: the correct UDI or UPC, or other device identification, the expiration date, the storage instructions, the handling instructions, and any additional processing instructions. 820.45(b) requires the release of labeling to be documented under Clause 4.2.5, and 820.45(c) requires operations that prevent mix-ups, including inspection of labeling and packaging before use against the medical device file, with the results documented.

The record that survives an inspection has one line per lot, showing each of the 5 elements checked, by whom, when, and against which revision of the medical device file. It shows label stock reconciliation and controlled storage of labeling, and it shows a change history, because label content changes flow through design change control under Clause 7.3.9 and into the medical device file, while distribution is evaluated through the initial consignee. It is important to note that this is a general description, and the specific evidence will depend on your process and your device.

So now you may be asking, how much of this can be automated? I want to highlight 3 situations where the QMSR lands differently, because these generate the most questions. For drug-led combination products, 21 CFR 4.4(b)(1) now lists ISO 13485 clauses in place of QSR sections for manufacturers using the streamlined approach. The clauses named include: Clause 4.1, Clause 5 and its subclauses, and 6.1, together with 820.10, then Clause 7.3 and its subclauses, Clause 7.4 and its subclauses, and Clause 8.2.2 together with 820.35(a), and then Clauses 8.4 and 8.5, Clause 7.5.3, and Clause 7.5.4 together with 820.35(b). Most Class I devices sit outside Clause 7.3 under 820.10(c), and that exclusion needs to be documented rather than assumed. Contract manufacturers, specification developers, relabelers, and the initial distributors of foreign entities are all "manufacturers" under 820.3(b), so the regulation reaches each of them directly. A contract manufacturer must document risk management in product realization under Clause 7.1 regardless of who owns the design, which FDA indicated at its town hall of January 14, 2026, as reported. A specification developer owns design and development along with supplier controls over its contract manufacturer, and an initial importer that performs no design need not apply Clause 7.3 but must still handle complaints, Medical Device Reporting, distribution records, and traceability. These are 3 common arrangements and not a complete map, and each firm documents its own applicability decision.

QSIT Is Gone: What Replaced It

The Quality System Inspection Technique, or QSIT, governed device inspections from 1999 until February 1, 2026, and it was built on 4 subsystems: Management Controls, Design Controls, Corrective and Preventive Action, and Production and Process Controls. It was a top-down approach, conducted either as a Level 1 abbreviated inspection or a Level 2 comprehensive inspection, and sampling tables prescribed how many records the investigator was to pull. The old section 820.180(c) exemption was written directly into the guide, which meant that management review reports, internal audit reports, and supplier audit reports were off the table.

Compliance Program 7382.850 carries an implementation date of February 2, 2026, and it supersedes both CP 7382.845 and the separate PMA inspection program, CP 7383.001, which means that PMA preapproval and postmarket inspections now run through the same process as everything else. It is a total product life cycle program. FDA states the goal as evaluating whether the quality management system meets FDA requirements and provides reasonable assurance that devices will be safe and effective, and whether risk management and risk-based decision making are effectively used.

There are 2 structural changes here that drive everything else in this section. The 4 subsystems are gone, replaced by 6 QMS Areas and 4 Other Applicable FDA Requirements, or OAFRs. And record review is now driven by identified product risk and investigator judgment rather than by sampling tables, with the program directing investigators to review "multiple records" in most cases.

The program also removes the fixed order of operations and asks the investigator to apply what FDA calls "critical thinking", which in practice means that evaluating one requirement may require evaluating other requirements elsewhere in the quality system. Investigators are expected to go beyond the stated minimum. And the records that QSIT exempted – management review, internal audit, and supplier audit records – are now squarely in scope.

What that combination does is remove the 2 features of QSIT that manufacturers had learned to prepare for, which were a predictable entry point at the top of a named subsystem and a predictable number of records. Under the new program the entry point is your own product risk documentation and the number of records is a matter of judgment, which is a very different preparation problem.

There are 2 additions to the program that are easy to miss because they do not sit inside the regulation at all. Cybersecurity for cyber devices under section 524B of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act is now part of the inspection, and so are Remote Regulatory Assessments conducted under section 704(a)(4).

The PIP breast-implant scandal exposed how little a scheduled surveillance audit could actually see, which led the European Commission to issue Recommendation 2013/473/EU, asking notified bodies to audit unannounced at least once every 3 years. The MDR, which is the European Union's Medical Device Regulation, then wrote unannounced audits into law under Annex IX, section 3.4, with a minimum of at least once every 5 years per manufacturer and an explicit right to extend those visits to critical suppliers and subcontractors. The notified body must keep a plan for these audits and must not disclose that plan to you, which means there is no version of this process where you negotiate the date, and the same expectation applies under the IVDR, the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation, for those of you on the diagnostics side.

In regards to FDA, domestic routine and for-cause inspections have always been unannounced, and the agency's inspection authority sits in section 704 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. What changed in 2025 is the announced expansion of unannounced inspections at foreign sites, which means the old assumption that "overseas means pre-announced" no longer holds for anyone. The QMSR, which is the Quality Management System Regulation at 21 CFR 820, has also been in force since 2 Feb 2026.

MDSAP, the Medical Device Single Audit Program, covers Australia, Brazil, Canada, Japan, and the United States, and those audits are normally announced and run on a 3-year cycle made up of an initial certification audit, 2 surveillance audits, and a recertification audit. However, the program does allow special and unannounced audits when a regulator requests one or when serious signals appear, so announced is the normal case and not a guarantee.

The fourth row is competent authorities and other regulators, and it includes the EU member-state authorities, ANVISA in Brazil, the TGA in Australia, and the PMDA in Japan. Notice from these bodies varies, and for-cause visits are often unannounced, which are typically driven by market surveillance activity, vigilance signals, complaints, or recalls. The last row is the one manufacturers forget, which is customers and distributors, and while those customer quality audits are usually announced and arrive through the quality agreements you have already signed, they are run against the same records an auditor would ask for.

The 2026 Regulatory Snapshot

In order to talk about audit readiness in any useful way, we first have to agree on what the regulatory landscape actually looks like in 2026, and there are 6 things I want you to carry in your head for the rest of this session. While all 6 of them will touch your quality system somewhere, the first 2 are where the majority of your readiness effort is going to land.

FDA QMSR

On 2 February 2026, the Quality System Regulation was replaced by the QMSR, which incorporates ISO 13485:2016 into 21 CFR 820 by reference instead of restating the requirements in FDA's own language. On top of that incorporation, FDA has added a small number of agency-specific requirements. The first, at 820.10, carries the general requirements for the quality management system. The second, at 820.35, covers records, including complaint and servicing records and the Unique Device Identification, or UDI, information tied to them. The third, at 820.45, covers labeling and packaging controls.

The Quality System Inspection Technique, otherwise known as QSIT, is retired, which matters to this room because a great many mock audit programs were built around the QSIT subsystems. It is important to note that the old exemption under 820.180(c), which kept management review records, internal audit records, and supplier audit records out of routine FDA review, did not carry over into the new regulation. Plan for investigators to ask for all 3 of those record sets, and plan for them to read what they are given.

EU MDR and IVDR

The extended transition dates under the Medical Device Regulation and the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation keep a large number of legacy devices in scope for years to come. Stipulated through Regulation 2023/607, MDR legacy devices run to the end of 2027 or 2028 depending on the device and the certificate, and under Regulation 2024/1860 the IVDR dates run from 2027 through 2029. However, unannounced audits continue regardless of transition status, under the same Annex IX provision we looked at a moment ago.

Alongside those dates, the duties of the Person Responsible for Regulatory Compliance, or PRRC, your post-market surveillance obligations, and the Periodic Safety Update Report, or PSUR, all remain live, and EUDAMED continues its phased roll-out.

MDSAP

MDSAP gives you one audit that serves 5 regulators, across the same 5 countries I named a moment ago, further jurisdictions participate as affiliates, and it is mandatory for Health Canada Class II through Class IV licences. Nonconformities are graded 1 through 5, and grades 4 and 5 are escalated to the participating regulators within 5 business days, which means a finding can be sitting with a regulator before your team has finished drafting a response.

United Kingdom

UK MDR 2002, as amended, remains the operative regulation in the United Kingdom, and CE marking is accepted there to 30 June 2028 for certificates issued under the old directives, the MDD, the AIMDD, or the IVDD, and to 30 June 2030 for certificates issued under the MDR or the IVDR. New post-market surveillance regulations have been in force since 16 June 2025, and manufacturers based outside the United Kingdom are required to appoint a UK Responsible Person.

ISO 13485 Itself

The standard sitting underneath all of this is still the 2016 edition, together with Amendment 1 from 2024, which adds climate change considerations, and it is the harmonised European version, EN ISO 13485:2016 with the A11 amendment of 2021, that carries the presumption of conformity under the MDR and the IVDR. A revision is under way in ISO/TC 210, so track the draft stages as they publish and expect a transition period rather than an overnight switch. I always recommend building a comprehensive transition plan once the draft stabilizes, instead of waiting for a published standard.

Other Major Markets

The remaining markets most of you deal with include Brazil under RDC 665/2022, the Brazilian Good Manufacturing Practices, Japan under MHLW Ordinance 169, China under NMPA GMP, Korea under KGMP, Saudi Arabia under its own SFDA requirements, and India under MDR 2017. Each of these is largely aligned with ISO 13485, which is the good news, and each of them carries local deltas on registration, records, language, and reporting, which is where the work actually is. Every date on this snapshot is current as of September 2026, and this is an area where dates move, so verify them against the source before you plan around them.

The Mechanics

An unannounced audit by a notified body is typically 2 auditors for at least 1 audit day, and it takes place either at your manufacturing site or at a critical supplier or subcontractor named in your technical documentation. There is no agenda in advance and the auditors expect to be admitted immediately, which in practice means that whoever is sitting at reception at 08:10 on a Tuesday is part of your quality system.

Delay is written into the report, and I want to be precise about that, because a badly handled arrival is not a neutral event. The time between the knock at the door and the opening meeting becomes a documented fact in a document you do not control. Refusal of access is grounds for suspension of your certificate. Product may also be tested on site in front of the auditors, or samples may be taken away for testing elsewhere.

There is one obligation in the mechanics column that manufacturers forget until it costs them, which is that you must have told your notified body when your lines will not be running. That covers holiday shutdowns and campaign manufacturing where a given product only runs for a few weeks in the year. If they arrive and nothing is being made, that is a wasted audit day for them and a significant problem for you.

The Focus

What they want to see is whether the certified device is being made here, and made as it was certified, which means units pulled from the line or from stock and checked against the technical documentation, traceability of critical components and materials, the recent design, process, or supplier changes and whether the notified body was notified of them, the validation status of the processes that are actually running that day, and interviews with the production and inspection staff.

That last item deserves a sentence of its own, because manufacturers prepare documents and they don't prepare people. The auditors will have conversations with the people at the bench, and the answer an operator gives about what they do when a part looks wrong either matches your procedure or it does not.

The callout at the bottom of the slide states it more plainly than I can. They are not there to read your quality manual. They are there to see whether the product being built today matches the product you certified.

The First 60 Minutes

In order to keep an unannounced audit from becoming a finding before it has properly started, it is essential that the first 60 minutes on site are governed by a written protocol and not by reaction, and the version in front of you is reproduced in full in the Participant Handout, which means nobody needs to copy it down. We will walk the 4 phases from left to right.

Reception

The first 5 minutes belong to whoever is sitting at the front desk. Identity is verified before anything else, which means photographic identification, agency or notified body credentials, and for an FDA investigator, Form FDA 482. Reception then makes exactly 1 call, to the Audit Response Lead or to the named deputy on the 24/7 roster, and then escorts and waits.

Auditors are never left unattended, they are never refused, and they are never stalled while somebody upstairs works out what to do. A laminated script at the front desk is the cheapest readiness investment you will ever make, and it is the one thing most sites do not have.

Mobilize

Mobilization is the phase where readiness either exists already or does not exist at all. Auditors are escorted to the audit room and offered water and wifi as per your own policy, while the notifications go out in parallel to the site head, to quality assurance and regulatory affairs leadership, to corporate quality, and to legal.

At the same time the request log is opened, the scribe, the runner and the subject matter experts are assigned by name, and the back room is established with the appropriate personnel, system access, and printing capability already in place.

Opening Meeting

The opening meeting is where the boundaries of the day are set, and manufacturers who rush it or skip it spend the rest of the audit negotiating from behind. We confirm the scope, the standard and the regulation being audited against, the sites included, and the auditors' own plan for the day. You then give the site overview along with the environmental health and safety and gowning briefing, which you owe them as visitors on your floor.

The logistics agreed in that room include the rooms themselves, printing, system access, your photo and sample policy, and the route by which document requests and findings will be communicated to you during the day. Agreeing that communication route at the opening meeting is what lets you correct a misunderstanding at 11 in the morning instead of discovering it at the closing meeting.

On the Floor

Once they are on the floor, the auditors select the product and the audit follows it. Every sample taken and every document requested is logged with a timestamp, which gives you the reconciliation you are going to need later that week. Your subject matter experts answer what is asked and then stop, while the scribe records every statement made in the room.

Runners retrieve the Device History Record, the Device Master Record and the validation records, and factual errors are corrected immediately and politely, at the moment they are made and not at the end of the day.

Global QMS Architecture: Core Plus Annex

Building a quality management system that holds up in every market at once is an exercise in deciding what has to be identical everywhere and what is allowed to be local, and the 4 tiers on this slide are how that decision gets written down. The organizing principle is that ISO 13485 is the spine, and that regulatory requirements are referenced rather than copied into your procedure text, which stops one market's change to one timeline from invalidating documents across the whole system.

The First Tier is the Global Quality Manual and Policies. This is one scope statement, one process map, and one site register, and I mean one of each, because the moment a site maintains its own quality manual you have created a second system that nobody reconciles.

The Next Tier is the Global Procedures, one procedure per process, each with a named global process owner behind it. The processes that belong at this tier include: complaints, corrective and preventive action, change control, supplier controls, design controls, document control, training, management review, and internal audit. A named owner is essential, because a procedure owned by a committee is a procedure that nobody keeps current, and divergence between sites is exactly what produced the systemic finding in Case 4.

The Third Tier is Where Locality Is Allowed to Live. Site work instructions describe how the work is physically done on that floor, with that equipment, and alongside them sits one Country Regulatory Annex per market which lists only the deltas for that market: the timelines, the forms, the authorities, the language requirements, and the roles.

Finally the Last Tier is Records and Forms, and the rule at this tier is one form per process globally. Local-language versions are controlled as translations and never as variants, because an uncontrolled local variant becomes a second process carrying the same document number.

A comprehensive governance structure is what stops the architecture quietly decaying between certification cycles, and the elements on the right include: global process owners, site quality heads accountable for Tier 3, a regulatory-intelligence feed wired into change control with an impact assessment completed within 30 days, a quarterly global quality council, and an annual review of the scope, the site register, and the requirements matrix. That 30-day impact assessment is the element that turns a regulatory change from an email somebody read into a controlled change.

Vigilance Reporting Timelines by Market

This is the table that Case 4 needed and did not have. Read across a single row, because the same event, reported by the same manufacturer, starts a different clock in every market you sell into, and some of those clocks run in calendar days while others run in working days.

Take the first row. In the United States, under 21 CFR 803, FDA requires a report within 30 calendar days for a death or serious deterioration, and 30 calendar days again for a reportable malfunction. Where remedial action is needed to prevent an unreasonable risk of substantial harm, the clock is 5 work days.

Move down to the European Union. Under Article 87 of the European Medical Device Regulation, the competent authorities work to 10 days for a death or an unanticipated serious deterioration, 15 days for other serious incidents, and 2 days for a serious public-health threat, and the MHRA in the United Kingdom holds to those same 3 clocks.

Health Canada, under SOR/98-282 sections 59 through 61, sets 10 days for a death or serious deterioration, and 30 days for an event that could lead to one if it recurred. The TGA in Australia works to 10 days for a death or serious injury, 30 days for near-adverse events, and 48 hours for a serious public-health threat. Japan's MHLW and the PMDA work to 15 days and then 30 days. Neither Canada nor Japan defines a separate public-health threat clock at all.

Brazil's ANVISA, under RDC 551/2021, is the one that catches people out, and it carries the shortest clock on this table: 72 hours for a death, 10 days for a serious injury, 30 days for other events, and 72 hours again for a serious public-health threat.

The design consequence is the part I want you to take away. A single global decision tree has to carry every one of these clocks, and for triage the shortest clock wins, which is why 48-hour triage is the design rule.

The Legal Position

ISO 14971 is not incorporated by reference into 21 CFR Part 820. Section 820.7 incorporates ISO 13485:2016, and it does not incorporate ISO 14971. In the Quality Management System Regulation final rule FDA was asked to incorporate ISO 14971 as well and declined, on the basis that the risk management requirements it needs are already captured through ISO 13485. That is the first half of the answer.

The Practical Position

The second half is the half manufacturers miss. Declining to incorporate ISO 14971 did not reduce the obligation, it relocated it. Risk management is enforced through the ISO 13485 clauses that Part 820 does incorporate, and those clauses include:

- Clause 4.1.2 b), which requires a risk-based approach applied to the control of the appropriate quality management system processes. This is an inspectable element in its own right.
- Clause 7.1, which requires risk management in product realization, with documented requirements and records of the results.
- Clauses 7.3 design, 7.4 purchasing, 7.5 production and 7.6 monitoring equipment, each of which carries risk proportionality. Manufacturers are required to size supplier controls, process validation and acceptance activities to the risk.
- Clause 8.2 on feedback, complaints and reporting, which uses post-market information as an input to risk management. This is the FDA analogue of Clause 10.

It is important to note that this list is a general list, and each manufacturer's process architecture will file those records in slightly different places.

Compliance Program 7382.850 lists "Risk-based Approach" under Management Oversight as an inspectable element. So the practical answer to the question of whether ISO 14971 is mandatory for FDA is that the standard is not, and the activity is. An observation is written against the clause, not against ISO 14971, and arguing the first half of that answer in front of an investigator without the second half goes badly.

Separately from Part 820, ISO 14971:2019 is an FDA-recognized consensus standard, so conformity to it can be declared in a submission. The entry is recognition number 5-125, ISO 14971 Third edition 2019-12, with the extent of recognition given as the complete standard. It entered the database on 23 December 2019 and was published in Recognition List Number 053 at 85 FR 17584 on 30 March 2020, replacing recognition 5-40 for the 2007 edition. It was still unchanged in Recognition List Number 066 of 24 August 2026. Recognition is not incorporation. This means that the entry supports a submission, however it does not create a regulation. ALARP and AFAP

There is one distinction in this section that changes how far manufacturers have to go, and it is the difference between ALARP and AFAP. The cleanest way to make it land is by what is absent from the regulation. "ALARP", as low as reasonably practicable, does not appear anywhere in the MDR. The MDR's only stated limit on how far a risk must be reduced is the one in Annex I point 2, which defines reduction "as far as possible", or AFAP, as reduction without adversely affecting the benefit-risk ratio. The Chain a Reviewer Expects to See

In order to estimate a risk that anybody can argue with, we have to agree on the four positions in the chain, and I am going to draw this on the board as I talk, because the picture is the whole teaching point. A hazard, defined at 3.4, is a potential source of harm, and on its own it does nothing at all. A foreseeable sequence of events is what turns that hazard into a hazardous situation, which at 3.5 is a circumstance in which people are exposed to the hazard, and only then can harm occur, harm being physical injury or damage to health at 3.3.

The two probabilities in your file sit at two different arrows on that chain. P1 is the probability that the hazardous situation arises, and P2 is the conditional probability that the hazardous situation goes on to lead to the harm, and the product of the two is the probability of occurrence of harm. Annex C.5 of the standard and Clause 5.5 of ISO/TR 24971 both describe that decomposition.

So now you may be asking, why do we bother separating the two? Because each half is defended with completely different evidence. P1 is engineering and field data, meaning failure rates, bench test results, field return rates, use frequency and exposure in the intended environment, and observed rates out of complaints and service data. P2 is clinical, meaning who is exposed and for how long, whether the harm is detectable before it becomes harm, whether it is reversible, and whether anyone intervenes in time.

Clause 10 and the Four Questions

Clause 10 has 4 subclauses, and each does a different job: 10.1 is general, 10.2 is information collection, 10.3 is information review, and 10.4 is actions. The MDR Plumbing That Clause 10 Has to Connect To

In the European Union, Clause 10 is not free-standing. It plugs into a named set of obligations under the Medical Device Regulation, or MDR, and in practice the notified body checks the joints rather than the pipes.

Article 10(2) is the headline, and it is one sentence: manufacturers shall establish, document, implement and maintain a system for risk management as described in Section 3 of Annex I. Article 10(9)(e) then puts risk management inside the quality management system as a named aspect it has to address, which is how it becomes auditable rather than merely required.

Annex I point 3, sub-points (e) and (f), is the loop written into the law itself. Manufacturers are required to evaluate the impact of information from production and from post-market surveillance on hazards, on the frequency of their occurrence, on risk estimates, on the overall risk, on the benefit-risk ratio and on risk acceptability, and then to amend the control measures where that evaluation tells them to.

Article 83(3)(a) makes updating the benefit-risk determination and improving risk management the first named use of post-market surveillance data, and Article 83(3) closes with "the technical documentation shall be updated accordingly." Annex II point 5 is where that lands, because the technical documentation has to contain the benefit-risk analysis in Sections 1 and 8 of Annex I, together with the solutions adopted and the results of the risk management under Section 3.

Annex III point 1(b) is the single most audited joint in the whole set, because the post-market surveillance plan must contain suitable indicators and threshold values used in the continuous reassessment of the benefit-risk analysis and of the risk management. Indicators and thresholds are quantitative, so if your surveillance plan has no numbers in it, that is a finding waiting to be written.

Three more provisions run through the same evidence. Article 86(1)(a) requires the PSUR to set out the conclusions of the benefit-risk determination throughout the lifetime of the device. Article 88(1) requires trend reporting where a statistically significant increase would change the benefit-risk analysis in Sections 1 and 8 of Annex I. Article 61(10) provides that where conformity based on clinical data is not appropriate, the justification rests on the results of the risk management, which is a heavier load than most files are built to carry.

Annex XIV Part B point 8 then sends the conclusions of the post-market clinical follow-up evaluation report back into both the clinical evaluation and the risk management. Recital 33 states that the risk management and clinical evaluation processes should be inter-dependent and regularly updated, which is what a reviewer cites when they ask why your risk file and your clinical evaluation report disagree.
